extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American journalism history; historians and researchers of early US press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards, practices, and practical constraints governing the production and evaluation of newspapers in the United States during the late 18th and early 19th centuries (roughly 1783–1835). Emphasis on press freedom, production/format, advertising, postal exchanges, legal-libel norms, materials, labor, and partisan practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of advertising and reading matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors desired abundant advertising revenue, but they had to provide a decent proportion of reading matter to keep circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors issued many "extras" and "postscripts" (often filled with advertising) to reconcile revenue needs and reader expectations; mercantile dailies sometimes used page one for advertising, sometimes saving only one column for reading matter. The Centinel’s practice and apology illustrate the tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising pricing and unit measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of measurement was the 'square,' counted at about twelve lines; the usual price in the larger papers was three shillings for the first insertion and two for the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising commonly included runaway slaves, apprentices, livestock, merchandise, liquors, books, real estate, lotteries, and ship sailings; mercantile dailies specialized in importers' announcements, vendues, theaters, legal notices, and sailings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising typography and display practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-column spreads, cuts, and large type broke up monotony about 1785; later shortage of paper and patronage pushed advertising typography back to small type and single-column measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York Daily Advertiser, Boston Independent Chronicle, Argus (New York), Aurora (Philadelphia) were notable for display lines and borders; later economic/ supply constraints drove design changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal exchange system as the heart of news-gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Postoffice Act of 1792 fixed postage and declared that 'exchanges' should be carried free; the exchange system was the heart of the news-gathering method of the papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free mailing of exchanges and low postage gave newspapers a vital postal standing; rescission or limitation would have destroyed the exchange system and forced many western papers to suspend publication. The Columbian Centinel praised the law as making exchange more sure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and reliability of mail as determinant of news delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mail schedules and conditions heavily influenced how quickly papers could circulate news (e.g., Philadelphia–New York in 22 hours three times a week; much longer to Lexington).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers were full of complaints of late mails; when roads were bad riders sometimes refused to carry papers, reducing timely distribution and affecting content freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter’s duty to protect news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the reporter's duty to protect his news source was established by instances of journalists refusing to divulge their sources and being arrested or held to custody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nathaniel Rounsavell of the Alexandria Herald (1812) was ordered into custody for refusing to divulge a source yet stood firm; similar arrests by the House in subsequent decades reinforced this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standard for libel defense: admission of truth and good motives
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial legal doctrine developed that the truth of an allegation must be admissible in evidence and that truth published with good motives could be a defense in criminal libel suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton's argument in the Croswell case urged admitting truth as a defense; New York legislature enacted statute enabling introduction of truth given good motives; by 1833 many states allowed evidence of truth for alleged libels dealing with public men, reducing criminal libel prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of abuse and calumny; adherence to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent advocates (e.g., Hamilton, Jefferson) deplored 'abuse and calumny' and urged recalling the press within the 'pale of truth'; unchecked scurrility and vulgar attack were criticized as a social pest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although scurrility and personal attacks were common in the period, contemporary critics argued that freedom of the press must operate within legal and wholesome limits of truth to preserve public trust and government stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan alignment and political advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly every publisher was compelled to take a side in personal electioneering; the press commonly functioned as partisan organs for political groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Tocqueville and contemporaries observed the press as a primary vehicle for political life; examples include sharply partisan Federalist and Republican papers and explicitly administration or opposition papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial quality and professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Though many newspaper men were printers with limited literary competence relying on unpaid contributors, the standard of editorship advanced during the period despite occasional vituperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some professional editors emerged even as many country editors depended on friends as 'contributors to the press' without fee; overall quality improved over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical format and production norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Most city newspapers enlarged to four- and five-column papers; wide columns, small type, and little display were common; four-page papers were the rule though 'postscripts' and 'extraordinaries' were used for emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheet sizes varied (crown, royal, super-royal); some frontier papers began smaller and enlarged when able; extras were a production practice to meet urgent news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource constraints: paper shortage limiting expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: A general shortage of paper constrained growth; papermills multiplied but hand production could not meet demand, sometimes forcing papers to reduce size temporarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper scarcity affected typography (smaller type, single columns) and limited overall expansion despite demand and increased literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipment investment and accessibility for starting papers
rubrics_metrics.description: A press and enough type to start a small paper could be procured at relatively small investment (about $200 to $800 at the end of the century), often using second-hand material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type founders and press makers (e.g., John Bain, Binny & Ronaldson, Adam Ramage) improved equipment availability and productivity; technological changes (Ramage screw press) slowly replaced older models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor standards and wages in printing trades
rubrics_metrics.description: Journeyman printers' standard wage was six dollars a week and twenty-five cents per 1,000 ems of composition; long hours and hard press work were common; occasional strikes and short-lived unions raised wages over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First printers' strike in 1786 won and dissolved; New York unions raised wages to $1/day in 1794 and $8/week in 1799; journeymen were sometimes wandering romantic figures in the trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversification of newspapers into job-printing and other publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Most newspapers conducted a business in job-printing and published pamphlets, almanacs, and books to supplement income and activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This diversification helped finance papers and broadened printers' businesses; many editors/printers were craftsmen running multifaceted print operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising content ethics and quality concerns (e.g., patent medicines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-medicine advertising increased and 'not a little of it clearly vicious'; testimonials were widely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rise of patent-medicine ads raised ethical and content-quality issues for newspapers; editors had to balance advertiser revenue with reputation and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and subscription pricing norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulations were generally small (e.g., Columbia Centinel ~4,000; Aurora ~1,700; averages 600–700), with dailies subscription rates from $6 to $10 per year (common price $8) and weeklies/semiweeklies commonly $2–$3 by 1800.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frontier papers sometimes accepted produce as payment; postrider carriage sometimes added a slight extra; single-copy readership in public venues (coffee houses, taverns) increased effective readership per copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extras/postscripts for emergency content and advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers issued 'Postscripts' and 'Extraordinaries' to meet emergencies; these extras were also often filled with advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Centinel explicitly used extras as compensation to reconcile advertiser generosity with readers' expectation of reading matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial conduct and risk during wartime/opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: During wartime (e.g., War of 1812) opposition newspapers could be outspoken but faced violent repression (mobs destroying printshops) in regions where the war was popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Baltimore mob wrecked presses of an anti-war paper; editors sometimes printed from other locations or relied on defenders; such episodes show the physical and political risks to partisan journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-provoked personal violence and dueling consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper paragraphs could provoke personal challenges, duels, and violence; the Hamilton–Burr duel famously followed publication and dispute over newspaper material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to editors were not uncommon, especially in South and West; duels and assaults illustrate social norms and the tangible stakes of printed personal attacks.
